summary: A 1975 note on the difference between early and later versions of FTP, arguing for leaving well enough alone. It is part of a discussion thread that includes RFC 691, RFC 640, RFC 630, RFC 542, RFC 454, RFC 448, RFC 414, RFC 385 and RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: Two versions of a tool worked a little differently. This note says do not change what already works well enough.

questions: early ftp versus later ftp differences
what did rfc 686 propose for ftp
subtitle: A newcomer's case for fixing the FTP everyone actually runs instead of waiting for a new version.

tldr.problem: Nearly every network host ran version 1 of FTP, yet people brushed off its quirks by pointing to the unused FTP-2 on paper.
tldr.mechanism: The author goes through eight claimed advantages of FTP-2, argues most are unneeded or can be achieved inside FTP-1, and proposes five specific FTP-1 changes plus a renumbering of reply codes.
tldr.outcome: No formal mechanism exists to adopt the plan, but the author bets that if TENEX makes the HELP change on June 1, the rest of the world will follow.

today: RFC 686 is a May 1975 opinion paper; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and it was followed by the slight revision in RFC 691. Treat it as part of a 1975 debate about FTP versions.

sections.title: Why Leave FTP-1 Alone
sections.content:
Brian Harvey, working on his site's FTP user and server programs, found that hosts did many things differently. When he asked, the answer from some quarters was "Oh, you're running version 1!" As far as he can tell, all but one network host run version 1 and transfer files fine.

His view is that an unused protocol on paper should not stop maintenance of the current one unless the new one is imminent or strongly superior. He then lists the main differences in FTP-2 and judges each.
sections.plainLanguage: He noticed everybody used the old version, and he thought that was good enough to keep improving rather than wait for a new one.

sections.title: Eight Claimed Advantages of FTP-2
sections.content:
The author weighs each point against FTP-2. Highlights:

  • FTP-2 uses TELNET-2, which allows flexible negotiation about echoing, but FTP partners are programs that do not want echoing.
  • On print files, the source already contains Fortran controls, so the recipient, not the server, should reformat them if needed.
  • The Network Virtual File System idea has pitfalls such as filename syntax differences.
  • More specific reply codes help the human, not the user program, so detail belongs in the reply text; RFC 640's numbering is more rational but can be mostly achieved without drastic reprogramming.
  • A committee having approved FTP-2 is no reason by itself to implement it.
  • Default data connection sockets are a security issue, which he illustrates with a story about a weekly password mailed to unprotected mailboxes.
  • FTP-2 being online while FTP-1 is not is a poor reason; retyping FTP-1 would cost less than everyone reprogramming.
  • MODE and STRU changes matter to few; he notes the TENEX paged-file work shows individual problems can be solved within FTP-1.
sections.plainLanguage: He goes down a list of reasons to switch and says, one by one, why each is either not needed or could be done with the old version.

sections.title: Reply Codes and the Proposed Fixes
sections.content:
A user program can almost interpret replies with a simple rule: replies starting with 0 or 1 are shown and ignored, 2 means success, 4 or 5 means failure, and 3 appears only for the initial 300 greeting, the 330 password request and the 350 mail response. The problem is HELP, which returns 0xx, 1xx or 2xx depending on the server, while STAT in practice sends lines coded 151 ending with 200 END OF STATUS.

His five requested changes:

  • HELP should return 200.
  • 1xx replies are informative status replies, neither positive nor negative acknowledgments.
  • Experimental reply codes take the form x9x or xx9, and codes above 599 are not permitted.
  • STAT with no argument requests a directory listing, or the transfer status if sent with TELNET SYNCH during a transfer; replies are zero or more 1xx messages then 200.
  • TYPEs P and F mean the file contains ASA control characters and the recipient reformats it if needed.

He also proposes moving many 4xx replies to 5xx, REQUIRED as of June 1, so mailers can tell temporary from permanent failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers answer with number codes, and the first digit tells a program what happened. He wants every server to follow that rule the same way, including a clear "all done" after help text.

sections.title: The Renumbering Table
sections.content:
The RFC ends with a list of current FTP-1 replies and their proposed new numbers. For instance, 201 (ABOR ok) becomes 251, 253 (rename ok) becomes 223, 254 (delete ok) becomes 224, 431 becomes 531, 450 (file not found) becomes 520, and 451 (access denied) becomes 521. A new 206 is adapted from RFC 640 for a superfluous command. The old 400 is dropped as unclear.

Changes from 4xx to 5xx are to be required as of June 1; second or third digit changes are described as not so important. The x2x and x5x meanings are interchanged to leave the 25x messages alone.
sections.plainLanguage: It finishes with a conversion chart showing which old number each message would change to.
